questions.title: How paediatric pharmacokinetics differ from adults
questions.question: Paediatric patients differ from adults in:

options.D: Having a less permeable blood-brain barrier

explanations.A: Correct. Neonates and infants have a higher proportion of total body water (about 70-80% of body weight versus roughly 60% in adults) and a larger extracellular fluid compartment. This raises the apparent volume of distribution of water-soluble drugs, so weight-based doses of hydrophilic drugs are relatively higher in children. It is the single true statement here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Neonates have LESS body fat than adults, not more; fat as a proportion of body weight rises through infancy but is low at birth, which is why lipophilic-drug distribution differs.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Plasma protein (albumin) concentrations are LOWER in neonates, increasing the free fraction of highly protein-bound drugs rather than being higher than in adults.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The neonatal blood-brain barrier is MORE permeable, not less, allowing greater CNS penetration of drugs such as opioids and bilirubin.

questions.learning_objective: State that paediatric patients have more total body water than adults, raising the volume of distribution of water-soluble drugs.

questions.title: Factors affecting drug dosage — the incorrect statement
questions.question: Regarding the factors affecting dosages of drugs, which of the following is INCORRECT?

options.A: Females need smaller doses than males
options.B: Irritant drugs must be given after meals
options.C: Renal glomerular filtration rate is decreased in geriatrics
options.D: Paediatrics have less body water and a less permeable BBB than adults

explanations.A: Correct statement (so not the answer). Women on average have smaller lean body mass and a higher fat fraction than men, so standard doses are often relatively larger per kilogram and modest dose reduction can be appropriate.
explanations.B: Correct statement (so not the answer). Gastric-irritant drugs (for example NSAIDs, iron, metronidazole) are given after meals to buffer the mucosa and reduce dyspepsia.
explanations.C: Correct statement (so not the answer). Glomerular filtration rate declines with age, so renally cleared drugs accumulate and doses of these must be reduced in the elderly.
explanations.D: Correct. This is the INCORRECT statement, and therefore the keyed answer: paediatric patients actually have MORE total body water and a MORE permeable blood-brain barrier than adults, the reverse of what is written. The other three statements are valid dosage-modifying principles.

questions.learning_objective: Identify correct dosage-modifying factors and recognise the false claim that children have less body water and a less permeable BBB.

questions.title: Therapeutic use of cholinergic agonists
questions.question: Which of the following is a therapeutic use of cholinergic agonists?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cholinergic agonists cause bronchoconstriction and increased bronchial secretion, so bronchial asthma is a contraindication, not a use.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Muscarinic stimulation slows the heart and lowers blood pressure; it is not used in and is hazardous after myocardial infarction.
explanations.C: Correct. Cholinergic agonists stimulate gastrointestinal smooth muscle and restore propulsive motility, so a direct agonist such as bethanechol (or the anticholinesterase neostigmine) is used to treat postoperative paralytic ileus and non-obstructive urinary retention. This exploits the parasympathomimetic action on gut and bladder detrusor muscle. It is the recognised therapeutic use among the options.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cholinergic agonists increase gastric acid secretion and would worsen a peptic ulcer, so this is a contraindication.

questions.learning_objective: List paralytic ileus and urinary retention as therapeutic uses of cholinergic agonists and recognise asthma and peptic ulcer as contraindications.

questions.title: Effect of anticholinesterases absent with parasympathetic nerve stimulation
questions.question: Anticholinesterases increase endogenous acetylcholine and mimic parasympathetic stimulation. Which of the following actions will appear ONLY with anticholinesterases but NOT with parasympathetic nerve stimulation?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bradycardia results from muscarinic action on the SA node and is produced both by vagal (parasympathetic) nerve stimulation and by anticholinesterases.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Increased gastric acid secretion is a direct vagal muscarinic effect and occurs with parasympathetic nerve stimulation as well as with anticholinesterases.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Miosis follows muscarinic stimulation of the sphincter pupillae and appears with both parasympathetic nerve stimulation and anticholinesterases.
explanations.D: Correct. Most resistance vessels have NO parasympathetic innervation, so nerve stimulation cannot dilate them; however their endothelium bears M3 muscarinic receptors that release nitric oxide. When an anticholinesterase raises circulating acetylcholine, it reaches these uninnervated endothelial receptors and produces vasodilation and hypotension, an effect the nerves alone cannot reproduce. Hence hypotension is the action seen only with anticholinesterases.

questions.learning_objective: Explain why hypotension appears with anticholinesterases but not with parasympathetic nerve stimulation (uninnervated endothelial muscarinic receptors).

questions.title: Lipid-soluble parasympathomimetic used as a miotic
questions.question: Which of the following parasympathomimetics has the greatest lipid solubility, passes the blood-brain barrier, and is suitable for use as a miotic?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acetylcholine is a charged ester that is hydrolysed within seconds by cholinesterase and penetrates membranes poorly, so it is unsuitable as a topical miotic.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Methacholine is also a quaternary choline ester with poor lipid solubility and little CNS penetration; it is used mainly as a bronchial-challenge agent, not a miotic.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Neostigmine is a lipid-insoluble quaternary anticholinesterase that does not cross the blood-brain barrier or penetrate the cornea well.
explanations.D: Correct. Pilocarpine is a naturally occurring cholinomimetic alkaloid and a tertiary amine, so it is lipid-soluble, crosses the blood-brain barrier and penetrates the cornea. This lets it be applied topically as a miotic that contracts the ciliary muscle and lowers intraocular pressure in glaucoma. Among the options it uniquely combines lipid solubility with a direct muscarinic action suitable for ocular use.

questions.learning_objective: Identify pilocarpine as the lipid-soluble parasympathomimetic suitable as a miotic.

questions.title: Best first step for postoperative urinary retention
questions.question: A 35-year-old woman recovering from abdominal surgery fails to pass urine. Which of the following is the best strategy?

options.A: Give an infusion of acetylcholine because it has a very short half-life
options.B: Give neostigmine because it will not have CNS side effects
options.C: Give bethanechol because it is selective to the urinary tract
options.D: Make sure she does not have urinary tract obstruction before giving any medication

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acetylcholine's ultra-short half-life makes it useless systemically, and giving any cholinomimetic before excluding obstruction is unsafe.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Neostigmine can be used for retention, but the justification is wrong and, more importantly, obstruction must be excluded first.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bethanechol has relative selectivity for bladder and gut but is not exclusively urinary, and it is still contraindicated if outlet obstruction exists.
explanations.D: Correct. The essential first step is to confirm there is no mechanical bladder-outlet obstruction before giving any cholinergic drug. Stimulating detrusor contraction against an obstruction can raise intravesical pressure dangerously and risk rupture or reflux. Only once obstruction is excluded is a cholinomimetic such as bethanechol appropriate, so safety adjudication precedes drug therapy.

questions.learning_objective: State that mechanical obstruction must be excluded before treating urinary retention with a cholinergic agonist.

questions.title: When atropine is preferred over its substitutes
questions.question: In which of the following situations is it better to use atropine rather than one of its substitutes?

explanations.A: Incorrect. For airway disease an inhaled, poorly absorbed antimuscarinic such as ipratropium or tiotropium is preferred over systemic atropine to limit side effects.
explanations.B: Incorrect. For fundus examination a short-acting mydriatic such as tropicamide is chosen so that cycloplegia and mydriasis wear off quickly, unlike long-acting atropine.
explanations.C: Correct. In organophosphorus (anticholinesterase) poisoning atropine is the antidote of choice because a broad, potent systemic antimuscarinic action is needed to reverse life-threatening bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm, bradycardia and secretions. The organ-selective substitutes are designed to limit systemic effect, which is exactly the opposite of what an antidote requires. Atropine, titrated to drying of secretions, is therefore preferred here over any substitute.
explanations.D: Incorrect. For bladder overactivity a uroselective antimuscarinic (for example tolterodine or oxybutynin) is used rather than non-selective atropine.

questions.learning_objective: Identify organophosphate poisoning as the setting where atropine is preferred over its more selective substitutes.

questions.title: Best use of hyoscine (scopolamine)
questions.question: Hyoscine would be most useful in the treatment of which of the following conditions?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Antimuscarinics tend to increase heart rate by vagal blockade, so hyoscine would aggravate rather than treat tachycardia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Central antimuscarinics impair memory and worsen cognition; Alzheimer's disease is treated with anticholinesterases (the opposite mechanism), not hyoscine.
explanations.C: Correct. Hyoscine (scopolamine) is a tertiary-amine antimuscarinic with strong central penetration, and it is the most effective agent for preventing motion sickness, classically delivered as a transdermal patch behind the ear before travel. Its action on central vestibular muscarinic pathways underlies this benefit. This central effect distinguishes it from the more peripherally acting atropine.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Antimuscarinics reduce gut motility and would worsen paralytic ileus, which instead responds to cholinergic stimulation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify hyoscine as the antimuscarinic of choice for motion sickness.

questions.title: Organophosphate effect not blocked by atropine
questions.question: A farmer exposed to insecticides (irreversible cholinesterase inhibitors) was given atropine. Which of the following effects of the cholinesterase inhibitor will NOT be blocked by atropine?

options.C: Increased lacrimal, salivary and mucous secretions

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bronchospasm is a muscarinic (M3) effect on airway smooth muscle and is blocked by atropine.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Increased gut motility and diarrhoea are muscarinic effects and are antagonised by atropine.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glandular hypersecretion is muscarinic and is reversed by atropine, which is titrated to drying of secretions.
explanations.D: Correct. Atropine blocks only muscarinic receptors, so it cannot reverse the effects at the skeletal-muscle neuromuscular junction, which are mediated by NICOTINIC receptors. The accumulated acetylcholine causes fasciculations, weakness and eventually depolarising paralysis of skeletal muscle, and these persist despite atropine. Managing the nicotinic component requires a cholinesterase reactivator such as pralidoxime and respiratory support.

questions.learning_objective: State that the skeletal-muscle (nicotinic) effects of organophosphates are not blocked by atropine.

questions.title: Drug added to neostigmine to reduce muscarinic effects in myasthenia
questions.question: The following drug is used with neostigmine to decrease the unwanted muscarinic effects in myasthenia gravis:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ephedrine is a sympathomimetic and does not antagonise muscarinic side effects.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Caffeine is a CNS stimulant/phosphodiesterase inhibitor and has no role in blocking neostigmine's muscarinic actions.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Azathioprine is an immunosuppressant used to modify the underlying autoimmune disease, not to counter neostigmine's acute muscarinic effects.
explanations.D: Correct. Neostigmine raises acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction to improve strength, but the same rise stimulates muscarinic receptors and causes salivation, colic, sweating and bradycardia. Atropine, a muscarinic antagonist, is co-administered to block these unwanted muscarinic effects while leaving the beneficial nicotinic action at the muscle end-plate intact. It is therefore the correct partner drug.

questions.learning_objective: Identify atropine as the agent used to counter the muscarinic side effects of neostigmine in myasthenia gravis.
